source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Tetris players make rotations and translations that do not advance the plan. The authors call these epistemic actions: moves that change the world to make thinking cheaper, faster or more reliable. They contrast them with pragmatic actions that move toward the goal.
numbers: A plan-first-then-act model predicts about half the possible rotations (1.5 for a piece with 3 possible rotations). Observed rotations exceed that for every zoid type (Fig 6, 95% CIs). Some rotations start before 100 ms, when the piece is not fully in view.
quote: actions are used to change the world in order to simplify the problem-solving task
limits: Small number of players; descriptive data. Cognitive Science 18, 513-549.
agent_relevance: Let the agent act on the world (run code, reformat, probe) as a cheap way to learn, not only to finish. Count such moves as useful, not waste.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) mental vs physical rotation cost
finding: Pilot mental-rotation test with Tetris shapes: reaction time rose linearly with angle difference, as in Shepard and Metzler 1971.
numbers: A physical 90 degree rotation takes as little as 100 ms (about 300 ms with button choice). Mentally rotating a zoid 90 degrees takes about 800-1200 ms. Three players (intermediate, advanced, expert), 8 presentations of each pair.
limits: Only 3 subjects; authors call it pilot data. Self-priming may shorten repeated mental rotations (their footnote).
agent_relevance: Where the environment can compute a step in about one eighth of the time, or exactly, hand that step to it. Simulating a transform in context is the slow path.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) translate-to-wall verification
finding: Players sometimes move a piece to the nearest wall and back before dropping it, to check which column it is in. The higher the drop, the more often they do it.
numbers: Fig 15: share of drops preceded by a translate-to-wall routine rises with drop distance (0 to 30 rows). At great height the cost of moving off the goal column is outweighed by the error it prevents.
limits: Descriptive plot; no inferential test in the passage read.
agent_relevance: An external check is worth its cost when an error is expensive. Pay for verification in proportion to the cost of being wrong (fits G3).

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) skill and epistemic action
finding: The authors argue chunking and compiled routines cannot explain the extra actions: players use them to expose information early and to prime recognition.
numbers: Rotation histograms (Fig 7): rotation begins in earnest by 400-600 ms into an episode and sometimes at the very outset.
limits: A search result says later UCSD work found some complementary actions decrease with skill. Not read here, so skill dependence is open.
agent_relevance: Do not remove external-probe steps just because a strong model is used. Test per task whether they still pay.

source: Zhang and Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks, Exp 1A/1B
finding: Four Tower of Hanoi isomorphs with the same problem space but different representations of the rules were solved with different difficulty. Times, steps and errors were normalised by minimum steps.
numbers: Experiment 1A: 24 UCSD undergraduates, four conditions (minimum steps 2, 4, 7, 8). Difficulty order was consistent across measures (Fig 10, Table 1).
limits: The PDF text is garbled OCR; design and ordering were checked, not every p value.
agent_relevance: Same task, different representation, different difficulty. How the program lays the problem out for the model is a main variable.

source: Zhang and Norman (1994) Experiment 2: externalising rules
finding: Moving rules from memory into the physical objects made the puzzle easier. Difficulty order: all rules internal (I123) > one external (I12-E3) = two external (I1-E23).
numbers: 18 subjects. Main effect of condition: p<.05 for times and steps, p<.005 for errors. I123 vs I1-E23 errors p<.001. I12-E3 vs I1-E23 not significant (p>.2).
quote: The more rules were external, the easier the problem.
limits: Small N. Rules were physically constrained (ring sizes, poles), so externalisation was enforced.
agent_relevance: Rules the program enforces cannot be broken. Put constraints into code or format, not into instructions the model must remember.

source: Zhang and Norman (1994) external rules are error proof
finding: Subjects made zero errors on external rules. All errors were on internal rules.
numbers: Experiment 2: all errors were for internal rules; none for external. The authors link internal errors to memory load.
quote: external rules seem to be error proof
limits: External rules were perceptually available or physically blocked, so this is a constraint effect as much as a load effect.
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G3: a check that refuses a bad move beats a reminder to avoid it.

source: Zhang and Norman (1994) Experiment 3: dimension representation
finding: Nine isomorphs coded the two dimensions with size, colour or location. For the ordinal dimension, location was significantly better than size and colour on time and errors.
numbers: 36 subjects, nine conditions, same three internal rules (Fig 16, Table 3).
limits: Exact p values not recovered from the garbled text.
agent_relevance: Order encoded by position (lists, tables) beats order encoded by a tag. Present ordered items by position.

source: Boldt and Gilbert (2019) Confidence guides spontaneous cognitive offloading
finding: People set external reminders more when they are less confident in their own memory, even when nobody told them to use reminders. Offloading raised accuracy in both groups.
numbers: 435 MTurk recruits, 72 excluded (N=363). Hit rate with offloading allowed 88.1% vs 82.7% without, F(1,361)=39.1, p<.001. Instructed group 87.2% vs spontaneous 83.8%, group effect ns (p=.18). Instructed group offloaded on about 53.1% of trials.
limits: Online sample; delayed-intention circle task; offloading is moving objects on screen.
agent_relevance: Trigger offloading on a calibrated low-confidence signal (G1), and let the agent find the offload move itself.

source: Risko and Gilbert (2016) Cognitive offloading
finding: Defines offloading as using physical action to change the information-processing demands of a task. Proposes a metacognitive account: people offload when they believe it beats internal effort, and the belief can be wrong.
numbers: Cites a short-term memory study in which people wrote items down about 40% of the time with only two items, where performance was already at ceiling without it.
limits: Review. The 40% figure is a secondary report of a cited study.
agent_relevance: The agent can over-offload (call tools it did not need). Gate tool calls on a signal and count their cost (G7).

source: Risko and Gilbert (2016) transactive memory and the internet
finding: Saving information on a computer can lower memory for it, and searching online can raise people's sense of their own knowledge. The review says this does not happen in all circumstances.
numbers: Names Sparrow et al. 2011 and work on cognitive self-esteem after using Google. No effect sizes in the text read.
limits: The Sparrow 2011 Google Stroop result failed to replicate (see a12).
agent_relevance: Do not design around the claim that offloading harms memory. The agent risk is over-trust in the tool, not forgetting.

source: Sparrow et al. 2011 failed replication (Camerer et al. 2018; PeerJ 2020)
finding: The Google Stroop effect did not replicate in the Camerer et al. 2018 multi-study project nor in a PeerJ replication. Sparrow argued the stimuli had dated.
numbers: Search snippets only. Effect sizes not retrieved.
limits: Not opened. No numbers.
agent_relevance: Treat the 'internet changes memory strategy' claim as weak. Do not cite it for the agent.

source: Martin and Schwartz (2005) Physically distributed learning
finding: Children aged 9-10 learned fraction concepts better when they could manipulate and adapt physical pieces. Adapting the environment lets new interpretations form, which advances learning.
numbers: Abstract and secondary citations only. The full text returned HTTP 403. No Ns or percentages recovered. SEP says children did better at 1/4 of 8 when they moved pie pieces than when they only viewed them.
quote: the opportunity to adapt an environment permits the development of new interpretations that can advance learning
limits: Not opened. Do not quote numbers. One thesis says pie pieces beat tiles; unverified.
agent_relevance: Learning in the environment needs the ability to rearrange it. Give the agent an editable scratch space, not a read-only context.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Embodied Cognition, section 2.2
finding: Defines embedded cognition: a task has a cognitive load and an agent can lower it by working in a well-designed physical or social setting. Gives Martin and Schwartz (pie pieces, 1/4 of 8) and Hutchins (navigating a Navy ship exceeds one person, so it is spread over specialists).
numbers: No numbers in the entry. Wilson (2004) pencil and paper multiplication as offloading.
limits: Encyclopedia summary; first 100000 characters read.
agent_relevance: This is the source of the design view in our brief: the program is the environment that holds the load.

source: Hutchins (1995) Cognition in the Wild, via Bazerman review
finding: Navigation on the USS Palau at Sea and Anchor Detail is done by a team of up to ten people on a cycle repeated about every three minutes. Two pelorus operators sight three landmarks, a recorder logs them, a plotter marks bearings with the hoey, a fathometer reads depth.
numbers: Up to 10 people; fix about every 3 minutes; three bearings give a triangle on the chart.
limits: Reviewer summary, not the book. No timing or error counts per step.
agent_relevance: Split a large job into small steps, each fit to one slot, with a shared written record between them. This is our state machine.

source: Hutchins (1995) tools change the task rather than amplify ability, via Latour review
finding: Latour quotes Hutchins: no component ability is amplified by a tool. Each tool presents the task as a different cognitive problem needing a different organisation of the same abilities. Cognition is a trajectory of representations across media.
numbers: Quote from p.154 of the book via the review.
quote: each tool presents the task to the user as a different sort of cognitive problem
limits: Latour's reading is stronger than Hutchins's. Not checked against the book.
agent_relevance: A tool changes which problem the model solves. Design tools so the leftover problem is one the model is good at.

source: Hutchins (1995) calculator in emergency fixes (second-hand)
finding: A search summary says that in the power-loss episode the team using a calculator was not faster or more accurate than without it.
numbers: No numbers. Unverified snippet.
limits: Not opened. Needs checking in the book.
agent_relevance: External tools do not guarantee a gain. Measure at equal tokens (G7).

source: Yao et al. (2023) ReAct
finding: Letting the model alternate thoughts with actions on an environment beats reasoning alone or acting alone.
numbers: ALFWorld: best ReAct trial 71% vs best Act 45% vs BUTLER 37%; worst ReAct trial 48% still beat BUTLER. Abstract: absolute gains of 34 points (ALFWorld) and 10 points (WebShop) over imitation and RL baselines.
limits: PaLM-540B and few-shot prompts; brittle when retrieval returns bad results.
agent_relevance: The core embedded-agent result: the world supplies facts and corrections that reasoning in the head cannot.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads
finding: A written scratchpad of intermediate steps lets language models do multi-step computation they fail at in one pass. It is an external working memory.
numbers: Polynomial evaluation: few-shot direct 8.8% vs scratchpad 20.1%; fine-tuned direct 31.8% vs scratchpad 50.7%. Program tracing: 11% and 20% direct vs 26.5% and 41.5% scratchpad (table partly garbled).
limits: Older models (up to 137B). The scratchpad is the model's own output, so it has no outside check.
agent_relevance: The scratchpad is the cheapest embedded environment. It helps most when steps are checkable by code.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces
finding: Designing the interface the model works in changes results. SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo solves 12.47% of 2,294 SWE-bench tasks vs 3.8% for the previous best non-interactive system, and 10.7 points more than a plain Linux shell on SWE-bench Lite.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite (300): full interface 18.0%; no edit action 10.3 (-7.7); edit without linting 15.0 (-3.0); no search 15.7; iterative search 12.0 (-6.0); file viewer 30 lines 14.3, full file 12.7, 100 lines 18.0. Claude 3 Opus: 10.5% of the full set.
limits: Single run per cell; Lite subset; design tuned on GPT-4 Turbo.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for the design view: environment details (linting guardrail, window size, summarised search) move success by up to about 8 points.

source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL: Program-aided language models
finding: The model writes a program and a Python interpreter runs it. This offloads the calculation and keeps decomposition for the model.
numbers: GSM8K: PAL 72.0%, about 15 points above PaLM-540B chain of thought (abstract: absolute 15% top-1). Table 1 is garbled in the text, so only the headline is recorded.
limits: PAL used Codex; baselines used other models. PAL averaged over 3 runs.
agent_relevance: Delegating exact steps to code is the cleanest offloading case. It matches our rule that the program counts and compares.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager
finding: A Minecraft agent with a skill library, iterative prompting on environment feedback and self-verification beats earlier agents.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, milestones up to 15.3x faster (wood), 8.5x (stone), 6.4x (iron). Removing self-verification cut discovered items by 73%. GPT-4 gave 5.7x more items than GPT-3.5 as code generator.
limits: Three runs per condition; prompting iterations as time unit; one game.
agent_relevance: Verification against environment state is the most valuable piece, as in G3.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: The agent stores verbal reflections on failed attempts in an episodic memory and retries. Reflection tied to real environment outcomes improves later trials.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. ALFWorld: +22 points absolute in 12 iterative trials. Ablation numbers were not read.
limits: Gains depend on informative feedback such as unit tests. Ablation numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: A persistent memory of real failures is an environment the agent writes to. Supports G2: revise from real output.

source: Sumers et al. (2024) CoALA: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents
finding: A formal frame for language agents: internal memory (working, episodic, semantic, procedural), an external action space grounded in environments, and a decision loop. The environment is a first-class part of the architecture.
numbers: No empirical numbers; framework paper.
limits: Conceptual; does not test the embedded framing.
agent_relevance: A vocabulary to map our states S0-S9 and operators to memory and action modules.

source: Mialon et al. (2023) GAIA
finding: Tasks needing tools (browsing, files) are easy for humans and were hard for a model with plugins.
numbers: Humans 92% (L1 94, L2 92, L3 87) vs GPT-4 with plugins 15%.
limits: Early 2023 models; later agents score much higher (not read here).
agent_relevance: Tool access alone is not an embedded-cognition win. The agent also needs the right loop and checks.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Reasoning models collapse on controlled puzzles past a complexity threshold. Giving the model the solution algorithm for Tower of Hanoi and Checker Jumping did not move the failure point much.
numbers: Figure 8: failures occur at similar complexity with and without the algorithm.
quote: Even when given the solution algorithm and only needing to execute prescribed steps, failures occur at similar points
limits: Contested paper (critics blame output limits and format); critiques not read here.
agent_relevance: Executing long procedures inside the model is unreliable. The program should execute the steps (be the environment) rather than ask the model to.
